To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sediment core BIAC072014, collected in a coastal area of the Humboldt Current System (HCS, Inglesa bay, 27°S), was used to reconstruct changes in biological productivity (BP) and ocean-climate variability during the last ~1.5 kya.

the changes in the productivity and the intensity of the OMZ in the Humboldt Ecosystem off northern Chile (Inglesa Bay, 27°S) are related to the regional intensification of coastal upweling, the regional cooling and the northward displacement of intermediate water subduction in the Eastern South Pacific.

“The changes in biological productivity, oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) and sea surface temperature (hereafter SST) during the last ~1500 years in Inglesa bay (27°S) were mainly controlled by changes in the oceanic circulation and the Walker cell.”
In summary, our research is concerned with

the reconstruction of oceanographic and climatic changes in the HCE during the last ~1.5 ka, and their influence on the biological productivity and OM2 intensity in a coastal environment of northern Chile.

the reconstruction of the changes in biological production and OMZ intensity and their relation with the ocean-climate fluctuations in the HCE during the last ~1.5 kya, and it is the first to provide a long-term record for the northern section of the HCE.

the reconstruction of changes in biological productivity, OMZ intensity and SST in Inglesa bay during the last ~1.5  kyr and the relationship between these parameters and oceanographic fluctuations in the HCE.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reduction in biological production and OMZ intensity was caused by the intensification of coastal upwelled water and a reduction of the detritic input.
the intensification of coastal upwelled waters during the last ~200 years did not cause a reduction of OMZ intensity and productivity in the northern section (~ 30°S) of HCE.

the reduction in biological production and OMZ intensity is related to a greater subsurface ventilation of the HCE, which is associated with the strengthening of the gyres and the northward displacement of subduction of the ESPIW.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in biological production and the OMZ in Inglesa bay are related to changes in the intensity of upwelling in this region.

, the changes in the biological productivity and oceanographic conditions in Inglesa bay during the last ~1.5 kya are related to changes in the regional oceanographic conditions and to changes in the oceanic and climatic conditions of the Southern Pacific Ocean.

the changes in biological production and OMZ intensity observed in Inglesa bay during the last ~1.5 k.yr. were mainly controlled by changes in the oceanographic conditions in the central zone (~ 30°S) and southern zone (~ 40°S) of HCE.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reduction in the OMz intensity and biological productivity in Inglesa bay during the last ~200 years is not associated with El Nino-like events.

the changes in the OMZ and biological productivity observed in the northern HCE are related to the changes in the regional ocean circulation and climate, and that the HCE acts as a transition zone between the coastal upwelling of the central HCE (~ 36°- 38°S) and the upwelling in the southern HCE (~ 14°- 18°S).

the changes in productivity and OMZ in Inglesa bay are not a simple response of the local coastal upwelling to the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, but a complex response to changes in the oceanographic structure of the HCE and its interaction with the South Pacific Gyre.
